summary: Retires the MD4 message digest algorithm described in RFC 1320 and explains the reasons, moving it to Historic status. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MD4 is an old way of reducing a piece of data to a short fingerprint. Weaknesses were found in it over the years, and this note explains them and tells implementers to stop using it in favour of a stronger, existing algorithm.

subtitle: Why the MD4 hash algorithm was retired and RFC 1320 moved to Historic status.

tldr.problem: MD4, published in 1992, has been under attack for years, and collisions and pre-images can now be found cheaply, yet it still appeared in various protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The document reviews the attacks, lists the RFCs that reference MD4 and the effect on each, and moves RFC 1320 to Historic status.
tldr.outcome: MD4 should be replaced by an existing hash algorithm such as SHA-256. The one notable impact is Microsoft's use of MD4 in RC4-HMAC.

today: RFC 6150 moves RFC 1320 to Historic status and is itself Informational, with no later RFC listed as obsoleting or updating it. It recommends SHA-256 or another existing hash algorithm instead of MD4.

sections.title: Introduction: What MD4 Is and Why It Is Retired
sections.content:
MD4 is a message digest algorithm that takes as input a message of arbitrary length and produces as output a 128-bit fingerprint, or message digest, of the input. This document retires MD4, and specifically moves RFC 1320 to Historic status, and the reasons for taking that action are discussed. The memo assumes familiarity with the companion hash attack document, which summarizes the use of hashes in many protocols and discusses how attacks against a message digest algorithm's one-way and collision-free properties affect, and do not affect, Internet protocols.

MD4 was published in 1992 as an Informational RFC. Since its publication it has been under attack, and in 1996 RSA suggested that MD4 should not be used. Microsoft made similar statements. Section 6 of the document discusses attacks against MD4 that indicate its use is no longer appropriate when collision resistance is required, and also discusses attacks against its pre-image and second pre-image resistance, together with attacks against MD4 used in message authentication with a shared secret, that is, HMAC-MD4.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash function turns any amount of data into a short fixed-length fingerprint, so that two different inputs should never give the same fingerprint. MD4 no longer guarantees that, so the note retires it and explains why.

sections.title: The RFCs That Referenced MD4
sections.content:
The document lists the RFCs in which the use of MD4 has been specified. As an Internet Standard there is RFC 2289, a one-time password system. As a Draft Standard there is RFC 1629, guidelines for OSI NSAP allocation in the Internet. As a Proposed Standard there is RFC 3961, encryption and checksum specifications for Kerberos 5, and as a Best Current Practice there is RFC 4086, randomness requirements for security.

Among the Informational RFCs are RFC 1760, the S/KEY one-time password system, RFC 1983, the Internet Users' Glossary, RFC 2433 and RFC 2759, the Microsoft PPP CHAP extensions in their first and second versions, RFC 3174, the SHA-1 document, RFC 4757, the RC4-HMAC Kerberos encryption types used by Microsoft Windows, and RFC 5126, the CAdES document.

There are other RFCs that refer to MD2, but they have either been moved to Historic status or obsoleted by a later RFC, so references and discussions about them are omitted, with the notable exceptions of RFC 2313, PKCS #1 RSA encryption version 1.5, RFC 2437, PKCS #1 version 2.0, and RFC 3447, PKCS #1 version 2.1.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists every specification that named MD4, so that each one can be checked to see whether it still depends on it. Most are old one-time password systems or Kerberos documents.

sections.title: Impact of Moving MD4 to Historic
sections.content:
The impact of moving MD4 to Historic is minimal, with one exception: Microsoft's use of MD4 as part of RC4-HMAC in Windows.

For the Draft Standard, Proposed Standard and Best Current Practice RFCs, the effect is small. The initial one-time password systems based on RFC 2289 have ostensibly been replaced by the HMAC-based mechanism of RFC 4226, which itself suggests following the recommendations of RFC 4086 for random input, and weaknesses of MD4 are discussed in RFC 4086. MD4 was used in the Inter-Domain Routing Protocol, where each message carries a 16-octet hash computed with MD-4, but IDRP was replaced by BGP-4, which required at least MD5. Kerberos Version 5 specifies the use of MD4 for DES encryption types and checksum types, but these were specified and never really used, and they are in the process of being deprecated, while the mandatory-to-implement encrypted types and checksum types specified by Kerberos are based on AES-256 and HMAC-SHA1.

For the Informational RFCs, PKCS #1 version 1.5 indicated there was no reason not to use MD4, while versions 2.0 and 2.1 recommend against MD4 because cryptoanalytic progress uncovered weaknesses in its collision resistance. The randomness requirements document mentions MD4 only to explain how the algorithm works and that there have been a number of attacks found against it. The Internet Users' Glossary provided a definition for message digest and listed MD4 as one example. The IETF one-time password specification was based on S/KEY technology, so S/KEY was replaced by OTP at least in theory, and S/KEY implementations in the wild have started to use MD5 in place of MD4. The CAdES document lists MD4 as a hash algorithm, disparages it, and then does not mention it again. The SHA-1 document mentions MD4 in its acknowledgements.

The three RFCs describing Microsoft protocols, RFC 2433, RFC 2759 and RFC 4757, are very widely deployed as MS-CHAP version 1, MS-CHAP version 2 and RC4-HMAC. MS-CHAP version 1 was supported in Windows XP, 2000, 98, 95, NT 4.0, NT 3.51 and NT 3.5, with support dropped in Vista, and version 2 in Windows 7, Vista, XP, 2000, 98, 95 and NT 4.0. Both are also supported by RADIUS and by the Extensible Authentication Protocol. In 2007, RFC 4962 listed MS-CHAP version 1 and version 2 as flawed and recommended against their use, and the memo reads those incidents as a strong indication of the need for built-in crypto-algorithm agility in authentication, authorization and accounting protocols. RC4-HMAC is supported in Windows 2000 and later for backwards compatibility, and although it does not rely on the collision resistance property of MD4, it uses MD4 to generate a key from a password, which is then used as input to HMAC-MD5. To recover the password an attacker first has to recover that key, and as RFC 6151 notes, key recovery attacks on HMAC-MD5 are not yet practical.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost nothing breaks. The protocols that used MD4 have either been replaced by newer designs or never relied on it in the first place. The one place it still matters is Microsoft's RC4-HMAC, which uses MD4 to turn a password into a key.

sections.title: Security Considerations: The Attacks
sections.content:
This section addresses attacks against MD4's collisions, pre-image and second pre-image resistance, and also attacks against HMAC-MD4. The memo notes that some may find the guidance on key lengths and algorithm strengths in the relevant NIST documents useful.

On collision resistance, a practical attack on MD4 was shown by Dobbertin in 1996 with a complexity of 2^20 MD4 hash computations. In 2004 a more devastating result presented by Xiaoyun Wang showed that the complexity can be reduced to 2^8 MD4 hash operations, and at the Rump Session of Crypto 2004 Wang said that, as a matter of fact, finding a collision of MD4 can be accomplished with a pen on a piece of paper. The formal result was presented at EUROCRYPT 2005.

On pre-image and second pre-image resistance, the first pre-image attack on full MD4 was accomplished with a complexity of 2^100, and some improvements are shown with certain pre-computations, where the complexity is reduced to 2^78.4 for pre-image attacks and 2^69.4 for second pre-image attacks. The pre-image attacks on MD4 are practical, so it cannot be used as a one-way function; for example, it must not be used to hash a cryptographic key of 80 bits or longer.

On HMAC, the attacks on hash-based message authentication code algorithms presented so far can be classified into three types: distinguishing attacks, existential forgery attacks and key recovery attacks, of which key recovery attacks are the most severe. The best results on key recovery attacks on HMAC-MD4 were published at EUROCRYPT 2008 with 2^72 queries and 2^77 MD4 computations.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of the three things a hash is supposed to guarantee have been broken for MD4. Two different messages can now be made to share a fingerprint, and a message can be reconstructed from its fingerprint, so MD4 can no longer be used to hide anything.

sections.title: Recommendation
sections.content:
Despite MD4 seeing some deployment on the Internet, this specification obsoletes MD4 because MD4 is not a reasonable candidate for further standardization and should be deprecated in favour of one or more existing hash algorithms, for example SHA-256. RSA Security considers it appropriate to move the MD4 algorithm to Historic status.

The memo gives the reason in plain terms: it takes a number of years to deploy crypto and it also takes a number of years to withdraw it, and algorithms need to be withdrawn before a catastrophic break is discovered. MD4 is clearly showing signs of weakness, and implementations should strongly consider removing support and migrating to another hash algorithm.

The document also mentions one non-IETF protocol: rsync once specified the use of MD4, but as of version 3.0.0, published in 2008, it has adopted MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: Stop shipping MD4 and move to an existing, stronger algorithm such as SHA-256. The advice is to retire a weak algorithm while it is still merely weak, not after it has already failed badly.

cells: Collisions can be found with a pen on a piece of paper
The first pre-image attack on full MD4
Key recovery, the most severe class of attack

viz.caption: THE PROPERTIES A HASH FUNCTION IS SUPPOSED TO HAVE

items.title: Collision resistance
items.text: Two different messages must not produce the same digest. This is the property the practical attacks broke.

items.title: Pre-image resistance
items.text: Given a digest, finding a message that produces it must be hard. The 2008 attack made this practical for MD4.

items.title: Second pre-image resistance
items.text: Given a message, finding a different message with the same digest must be hard.

items.title: HMAC key recovery
items.text: Attacks on HMAC-MD4 come in three kinds: distinguishing, existential forgery and key recovery, the last being the most severe.
